opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's an interesting question, because I think the extended mind thesis is kind of the odd one out among the four E's. Embodied, embedded, and enactive cognition are, in a sense, fairly modest once you strip away some of the rhetoric. They say that cognition doesn't happen in a vacuum, that the body and the environment shape how we think, and that you can't fully understand a cognitive system without looking at how it's coupled to the world. I think almost everyone should accept some version of that.

The extended mind thesis, at least in the original Clark and Chalmers formulation, makes a stronger and more metaphysical claim. It isn't just that the environment *influences* cognition. It's that cognitive processes, and even mental states like beliefs, can literally be partly constituted by things outside the skull. The classic example is Otto and his notebook. Otto has Alzheimer's, he writes down the address of the museum, and the claim is that the notebook entry plays the same functional role as Inga's biological memory, so Otto genuinely *believes* the museum is on 53rd Street, in virtue of the notebook.

I'm actually fairly sympathetic to that, and the reason is that I'm a pretty committed functionalist. If you think mental states are individuated by their functional roles, then where the physical substrate happens to sit is arbitrary. The skin and skull aren't magic. If the parity principle holds, meaning a process would count as cognitive if it happened in the head, then it should count as cognitive when it happens outside the head too.

Where I'd push back a little is on how the thesis sometimes gets bundled into 4E as though it's part of an anti-computationalist or anti-representationalist package. I don't think it is. Extended mind is, if anything, a very functionalist, very computational idea. It works naturally with the view that the mind is an information-processing system, just one whose boundaries are fuzzier than we assumed. So I think there's tension when people use it alongside strong enactivist claims that reject representation altogether. Those are pretty different philosophical motivations.

This also matters a lot for how we think about AI. People routinely say a language model "doesn't really know" something because it retrieved it from a tool, a database, or its context window, as if knowledge has to live in the weights to count. From an extended mind perspective that distinction looks much less principled. A model with reliable retrieval it routinely trusts and uses arguably knows that information in the same sense Otto knows where the museum is. So I think extended mind is one of the more useful parts of the 4E picture. It just belongs more naturally in the functionalist camp than in some of the company it keeps.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the extended mind thesis as one of the four E’s, but it does not mention an ecological interpretation or identify a debate between the extended and ecological views.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the extended mind thesis is interesting because it's often lumped in with 4E cognition, but I actually think it sits a bit awkwardly with the other three. Embodied, embedded, and enactive cognition are all, in a sense, claims about how cognition depends on the body and the environment. Extended mind, in the Clark and Chalmers version, goes a step further and says the environment can literally be part of the mind. Otto's notebook is part of his memory, not just a tool his memory uses.

I'm somewhat sympathetic to it, but I think a lot of the debate is really a verbal dispute about where to draw the boundary of the word "mind." If you're a functionalist, which I broadly am, then the natural thing to say is that what makes something a cognitive process is the functional role it plays, not whether it happens to be inside the skull. And once you accept that, the extended mind follows pretty straightforwardly, because nothing about the skull boundary is doing any explanatory work. The notebook plays the same role the hippocampus would.

Where I think it gets more interesting, and more relevant to what we work on, is in how it reframes questions about AI systems. People will say a language model doesn't "really" know something because it's retrieving it from a context window or a tool call rather than from its weights. But that's exactly the move the extended mind thesis is designed to challenge. If the retrieval is reliable, readily available, and automatically endorsed, which are roughly Clark's criteria, then it's not clear why we should privilege the weights. The weights are just one substrate. In some sense the whole system, including the scaffolding around it, is the cognitive agent.

The place I'd push back on the 4E crowd is that they sometimes use the extended mind as a stick to beat computationalism with, as if externalizing cognition shows it isn't computation. I think that's backwards. The thesis is most natural precisely if you think cognition is computation, because computation is the kind of thing that can be distributed across arbitrary physical substrates. So I'd include it in 4E, but I'd want to detach it from the anti-representationalist baggage that often comes along for the ride.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether extended mind belongs in 4E cognition, but it does not identify a debate over whether the disputed E means “extended” or “ecological.”

astra-6.text:
I think the extended mind thesis is a little bit of an odd fit within 4E cognition, because it’s quite compatible with computational functionalism. You can think that cognition is computation and also think that some of that computation happens outside the skull. There’s no contradiction there.

Take the familiar example of someone using a notebook as a memory aid. The question is whether the notebook plays a sufficiently integrated role in their cognitive life that we should count it as part of their memory system. That’s a question about where the system’s boundaries are, rather than a rejection of computation or representation.

So I’d want to distinguish those claims. Embodiment, embeddedness, enaction, and extension get grouped together, but they don’t necessarily stand or fall together. You could accept that cognitive processes extend into the environment without accepting the stronger anti-representational claims associated with some versions of enactivism.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the extended mind thesis and whether cognition can extend beyond the skull, but it does not identify a debate over whether the disputed 4E term should mean “extended” or “ecological.”

sol-6.1.text:
I’m a bit skeptical of grouping the extended mind thesis together with the other E’s, because it seems like a different kind of claim. Embodiment and embeddedness can be claims about how cognition works—how your body and environment influence the computations you perform. The extended mind thesis asks whether some of that environment literally counts as part of your mind.

You can agree that a notebook or a computer is essential to how someone solves a problem without agreeing that it’s part of their cognitive system. There’s a distinction between something being causally important and something being constitutive of cognition. And I’m not sure that deciding where to draw that boundary necessarily gives us a better explanation of the process.

So I’d want to separate the empirical questions about how these systems interact from the question of what we’re willing to call a mind.
